attribution.note: Marcus credits Tim Estes for raising the point but states the claim in his own voice and endorses it.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both the 'if… really is' premise about the alleged prompt and the 'not always' scope. It describes present behaviour, so observation is the right kind.

contract.note: Requiring proof that the alleged instructions actually governed the sessions respects his conditional premise. One verified violation is enough for 'not always', which is a fair, ordinary reading. The Jan 1–Feb 15, 2024 window is inferred, not stated.

evidence.note: A contemporaneous extraction report giving the alleged prompt's text. It does not authenticate the prompt and does not tie any output to a violation.
An earlier, October 2023 extraction of a different prompt version. It notes the prompt was never officially confirmed and records no violation.

reviews.rationale: The packet neither authenticates the alleged February prompt nor pairs it with any dated ChatGPT output that breaks it. The premise and the claimed violation both remain unverified, so the evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own authorial statement in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully restates his firm present-tense claim that programming in English with LLMs doesn't yet work that well.

contract.note: Reading the claim as about dependable, correct completion of clearly specified programming requests is fair and ordinary. It avoids both the 'any ability at all' reading and requiring a near-total failure rate. The time window is chosen by the evaluator.

evidence.note: A January 2024 primary evaluation: GPT-4 with direct prompting solved 19% of clearly specified CodeContests problems (pass@5), and 44% only with an iterative test-and-repair flow. That meets the support condition. Caveat: these are competitive-programming problems, not everyday programming.
A December 2023 refactoring benchmark that documented lazy, incomplete code. It falls before the window and the tasks were chosen to be hard, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: A contemporaneous primary evaluation shows GPT-4 failing most clearly specified programming tasks under direct prompting, with testing and repair needed to improve results. The packet has no broad evaluation showing dependable completion. The evidence is narrow (competitive problems), but it meets the contract's support condition for a modest claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion about examples he co-described with Southen and Conrad.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'much of' scope, the reference to the recently described examples, and the fact that the directives are alleged.

contract.note: Reading 'much' as a substantial portion and requiring proof the directives applied to ChatGPT sessions are reasonable readings. Leaving out Midjourney and Bing examples fits his phrase 'those directives'. The example set and the time window are inferred.

evidence.note: Gives the text of the alleged directives, including the rules against naming or describing copyrighted characters and against discussing copyright. It does not show those directives governed the January sessions.

Independent January 2024 tests showing ChatGPT refusals that mention copyright, plus recognizable characters produced from indirect requests. These are not the examples Marcus refers to, and instruction applicability is unverified.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no corroborated list of the Marcus/Southen/Conrad examples, no evidence the alleged February prompt applied to them, and no rewritten DALL-E prompts. The Tom's Hardware tests are suggestive but cover different examples. Whether a substantial share flagrantly violated the directives cannot be determined.
